hmmt-feb-2019-geo-01.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-01.body:
The angles sum to $360^\circ$. If three angles were at least $120^\circ$, the fourth would be at most $0^\circ$, impossible; so every quadrilateral has at least two angles below $120^\circ$, and $d=120$ works. For any $d<120$ pick $\alpha$ with $d\le\alpha<120$: a (possibly non-convex) quadrilateral with angles $\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,360^\circ-3\alpha$ has only one angle below $d$. So the minimum is $d=120$.

**Answer: 120**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-02.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-02.body:
$AECF$ is a parallelogram ($AF\parallel CE$, $AE\parallel CF$). Equal areas of the three pieces give $BE=DF=\frac13AB$. Let $X=CE\cap BD$. As $BE\parallel CD$, $\frac{EX}{XC}=\frac{BE}{CD}=\frac13$. In right triangle $EBC$ with altitude $BX$, $BX^2=EX\cdot XC=3EX^2$, so $\tan\angle EBX=\frac{EX}{BX}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, i.e. $\angle ABD=30^\circ$. Then $\angle BEC=60^\circ$ and $CE=2BE=\frac23AB=AE=CF$. Since $\angle ECF=\angle BEC=60^\circ$, triangle $CEF$ is equilateral, so $CF=EF=1$ and $AB=\frac32$. Hence $BD=\frac{AB}{\cos30^\circ}=\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-03.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-03.body:
For fixed $X$, the points $P$ with $AX=2PX$ form the circle of radius $\frac12AX$ centered at $X$. As $X$ runs over $AB$ these circles sweep out the region $S$. The largest circle is $\omega$ with center $B$ and radius $1$, and the largest angle $\angle PAB$ over points of the circle centered at $X$ is $\arcsin\frac12=30^\circ$ (tangent from $A$), for every $X$. So $S$ is bounded by the two tangent lines from $A$ to $\omega$ and by $\omega$.

Let $Q,Q'$ be the tangent points from $A$ to $\omega$. Triangles $AQB$ and $AQ'B$ are $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles with hypotenuse $2$, each of area $\frac{\sqrt3}2$. The rest of $S$ is the $240^\circ$ sector of $\omega$ bounded by $BQ$ and $BQ'$ (the side away from $A$), of area $\frac23\pi$. So $[S]=\sqrt3+\frac{2\pi}3$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3+\frac{2\pi}{3}$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-04.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-04.body:
Triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$ are each half a parallelogram, so each has area $84$. Hence $B$ and $C$ are at the same distance from $AD$, on the same side (convexity), so $BC\parallel AD$ and $ABCD$ is a trapezoid. Then $[ABG]=[CDG]=x$, $[BCG]=x-10$, $[ADG]=84-x$.

Because $\frac{[ABG]}{[CBG]}=\frac{AG}{GC}=\frac{[ADG]}{[CDG]}$, we get $\frac{x}{x-10}=\frac{84-x}{x}$, so $x^2-47x+420=0$, $x=12$ or $35$.

The hexagon is twice the trapezoid: $2[x+(x-10)+(84-x)+x]=4x+148$. The smaller value, at $x=12$, is $196$.

**Answer: 196**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-05.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-05.body:
Let $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=\beta$. Reflection gives $\angle DBA=\angle CBA=\beta$. Since $AO$ is the axis of symmetry, $\angle BAO=\frac12\angle BAC=90^\circ-\beta$, so $\angle ABO=90^\circ-\beta$. Hence $\angle DBO=\beta+(90^\circ-\beta)=90^\circ$ and $BC=BD=\sqrt{DO^2-OB^2}=\sqrt2$.

Then $\angle BOC=90^\circ$ and $O$ is at distance $\frac{\sqrt2}2$ from $BC$. The apex $A$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at distance $1+\frac{\sqrt2}2$ from $BC$ (same side as $O$, the intended acute triangle) or $1-\frac{\sqrt2}2$ (other side). The area is $\frac12\cdot\sqrt2\left(1\pm\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)=\frac{\sqrt2\pm1}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2}$** (the obtuse configuration gives $\frac{\sqrt2-1}{2}$)

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-06.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-06.body:
The centers form an equilateral hexagon of side $2$, and the radius of $C$ is $1+\rho$ where $\rho$ is the radius of the smallest circle containing the six centers. So $R-r=\rho_{\max}-\rho_{\min}$.

**Minimum.** If $\rho<2$ and all centers are within $\rho$ of a point $O$, then in each triangle $O_iOO_{i+1}$ the side $O_iO_{i+1}=2$ is the longest, so $\angle O_iOO_{i+1}>60^\circ$ for all six $i$; these angles total at most $360^\circ$, a contradiction. So $\rho\ge2$, with equality for the regular hexagon: $r=3$.

**Maximum.** Take four centers at the vertices of a square of side $2$ ($C_1,C_3,C_4,C_6$) and place $C_2$ and $C_5$ as apexes of equilateral triangles of side $2$ on two opposite sides (pulled apart). The enclosing circle of the centers then has radius $\sqrt3+1$, so $R=2+\sqrt3$. This is the largest possible: for hexagon $ABCDEF$ of centers, centering at the midpoint $O$ of the longest diagonal $AD$ works because for $B$, with $M$ the midpoint of $AC$, $BM\le\sqrt3$ and $MO=\frac{CD}2=1$, so $OB\le\sqrt3+1$; similarly for the other vertices.

Therefore $R-r=2+\sqrt3-3=\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3-1$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-07.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-07.body:
The circumcircle of $AHB$ is the reflection of the circumcircle of $ABC$ in $AB$, so it has radius $R=\frac{abc}{4K}=\frac{13\cdot14\cdot15}{4\cdot84}=\frac{65}8$. The same holds for $BHC$ and $CHA$. All three circles pass through $H$, each with radius $R$. The circle centered at $H$ with radius $2R$ is tangent to each of them at the antipode of $H$ in that circle. So the required radius is $2R=\frac{65}{4}$.

**Answer: $\frac{65}{4}$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-08.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-08.body:
Place $B(-\frac12,0)$, $C(\frac12,0)$, $A(a,b)$ with $b>0$. The midpoint $N$ of $OH$ is the nine-point center, equidistant from the midpoints $M=(0,0)$ of $BC$, $E$ of $AC$ and $F$ of $AB$. It lies on the perpendicular bisector of $EF$, whose $x$-coordinate is $\frac a2$; since $N$ is on $BC$, $N=(\frac a2,0)$.

$MN=EN$ gives $\frac{a^2}4=\frac1{16}+\frac{b^2}4$, so $a^2=b^2+\frac14$. The perimeter gives $AB+AC=5$, i.e. $\sqrt{2a^2+a}+\sqrt{2a^2-a}=5$ (using $(a\pm\frac12)^2+b^2=2a^2\pm a$). Isolate and square: $25-2a=10\sqrt{2a^2-a}$, so $625-100a+4a^2=200a^2-100a$, giving $a^2=\frac{625}{196}$. Then $b^2=\frac{625}{196}-\frac{49}{196}=\frac{576}{196}$, $b=\frac{12}7$, and the area is $\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac{12}{7}=\frac67$.

**Answer: $\frac67$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-09.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-09.body:
Put $A$ at the origin with $AD$ the $x$-axis, $AB$ the $y$-axis, $AE$ the $z$-axis. The plane is $z=k_1x+k_2y$. Since $AP=AS$ and $AB=AD$, $PB=SD$, so $P(0,6,6k_2)$ and $S(6,0,6k_1)$ have the same height: $k_1=k_2=k$. Then $Q$ and $R$ have $z=49$: $Q(\frac{49}k-6,6,49)$, $R(6,\frac{49}k-6,49)$. The condition $QR^2=RS^2$ becomes $(49-6k)^2(k^2+1)=2(49-12k)^2$, i.e. $(k-7)(36k^3-336k^2-203k+343)=0$. For $Q,R$ to lie on the edges we need $\frac{49}{12}\le k\le\frac{49}6$, and the cubic has no root there, so $k=7$.

Project $APQRS$ onto the base $ABCD$: it covers the square minus a right isosceles triangle with legs $12-\frac{49}{k}=5$, area $36-\frac{25}2=\frac{47}2$. The plane has normal $(k,k,-1)$, so $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt{2k^2+1}}=\frac1{\sqrt{99}}$. Hence $[APQRS]=\frac{47}{2}\sqrt{99}=\frac{141\sqrt{11}}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{141\sqrt{11}}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2019-geo-10.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2019-geo-10.body:
Use complex numbers: a rotation by $\pm90^\circ$ is multiplication by $\pm i$, which gives every vertex explicitly in terms of $a,b,c$ (e.g. $B_2=b(1+i)-ci$, $C_1=bi+c(1-i)$). The structure that results:

- $B_2C_1C_4B_3$ (and its two cyclic analogues) is a trapezoid with parallel sides $BC$ and $4BC$ and height equal to the altitude $h_a$ from $A$, so its area is $\frac{5BC}{2}h_a=5[ABC]$.
- The outer squares have sides $4BC$, $4CA$, $4AB$. Extending $B_5B_4$ and $B_6B_3$ to meet at $B_7$ gives triangles $B_7B_4B_3\cong BB_1B_2$ and $B_7B_5B_6$ similar to them with ratio $1:5$. Since $[BB_1B_2]=[ABC]$ (the angles $\angle B_1BB_2$ and $\angle ABC$ are supplementary), $[B_3B_4B_5B_6]+[BB_1B_2]=25[ABC]$, and similarly at $A$ and $C$.

Adding up the regions: $[ABC]$, the three trapezoids ($15[ABC]$), the three $25$-pieces ($75[ABC]$) account for $91[ABC]$ in total, and the squares not already covered contribute $20(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2)$: the three squares on the sides give $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2$, the second-layer squares have $A_1A_2^2=2AB^2+2AC^2-BC^2$ etc. totalling $3(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2)$, and the outer squares total $16(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2)$. So
$$[A_5A_6B_5B_6C_5C_6]=91[ABC]+20(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2)=91\cdot84+20\cdot590=7644+11800=19444.$$

**Answer: 19444**
